title: Krylov Edge Spectroscopy of Symmetry-Protected Topological Phases
abstract: We introduce $Krylov$ $edge$ $spectroscopy$, a many-body operator-space protocol for detecting and classifying one-dimensional symmetry-protected topological phases from local boundary dynamics. A Hermitian boundary operator generates a semi-infinite Krylov hopping chain whose boundary weight obeys an exact zero-frequency normalizability criterion. Open-periodic, boundary-bulk, and symmetry-preserving boundary-perturbation tests identify protected boundary memory, while a finite-depth leakage residual certifies when an explicitly reconstructed operator is already near zero frequency. Classification minimizes the normalized commutator over symmetry-resolved boundary operators in fixed charge sectors. For bosonic $\mathbb{Z}_N \times \mathbb{Z}_N$ phases, the recovered endpoint charge gives the cohomology label. The method requires neither many-body exact diagonalization, an explicit ground-state wavefunction or entanglement spectrum, nor a guessed dressed edge or string operator. For finite-range Hamiltonians, locality organizes the thermodynamic limit at fixed Krylov depth before the depth limit. We demonstrate the protocol in cluster, clock, Haldane, and trivial spin-1 chains. In the exactly solvable cluster chain, the transition between the gapped topological and trivial phases manifests as a localization-delocalization transition of the Krylov edge mode on the Krylov chain. This transition occurs precisely at the bulk gap closing, and its localization-length exponent coincides with the Ising correlation-length exponent. Through operator Krylov dynamics, our work turns local boundary evolution into a direct spectroscopy of many-body topology.
summary: The authors present Krylov Edge Spectroscopy, a novel, local diagnostic tool to characterize Symmetry-Protected Topological phases in 1D quantum systems. By analyzing the spectral properties of boundary operators via Krylov recursion, the method detects topological protection without requiring full diagonalization. This technique successfully classifies phases by relating boundary dynamics to fundamental topological invariants like cohomology labels.
main_problem: The paper introduces Krylov Edge Spectroscopy to develop a method for detecting and classifying one-dimensional Symmetry-Protected Topological (SPT) phases.
main_result: The method successfully maps the transition between topological and trivial phases to a localization-delocalization transition of the Krylov edge mode, and it can recover exact cohomology labels for models like the clock chain.
method: It uses a many-body operator-space protocol based on Krylov recursion applied to local boundary observables, avoiding the need for exact diagonalization or entanglement spectra.
model_or_system: The analysis is performed on one-dimensional systems, including cluster, clock, Haldane, and spin-1 chains, using finite-range Hamiltonians in the Gibbs state.
key_observables: Zero-frequency normalizability criterion, boundary ratios ($R_K, B_K$), leakage residual ($\epsilon_K$), and the minimum stiffness ($\kappa_{\min}$) for classification.
important_parameters: The Krylov depth ($K$), the system size ($L$), and the symmetry group structure ($\mathbb{Z}_N 	imes \mathbb{Z}_N$ or $D_2$).
main_assumptions: The method assumes the existence of a unique self-adjoint realization for the infinite tridiagonal operator and relies on the exponential locality of 1D Gibbs states.
paper_structure: The paper follows a logical progression: first, establishing the theoretical framework via Krylov recursion and boundary tests for detection; second, detailing the classification procedure by minimizing local commutator norms across symmetry sectors; and finally, demonstrating the protocol's success on benchmark models like the clock and spin-1 chains.
why_interesting: This provides a powerful, purely local, and computationally tractable diagnostic tool to probe global topological invariants in 1D quantum systems, which is highly relevant for understanding boundary physics in condensed matter systems.
